faq.answer: We hand over everything: access, passwords, documentation and the ticket history. Infrastructure that cannot be passed to another contractor without us is not a service, it is a lock-in, and we do not work that way.

infosecAudit.lead: We assess the security of the whole company rather than a single website: network and servers, access rights, backups, mail, workstations and how people handle data. What you get is a report with risk levels and a plan of what to fix first.

Checking the network, servers and workstations for known vulnerabilities

faq.question: How is this different from a website security audit?
faq.answer: In scale and in subject. A website audit checks one web application: code, access, dependencies, server settings. This checks the company: network, servers, workstations, rights, backups and how the processes are built. One does not replace the other, and both are often needed.

faq.question: Will you just run a scanner?
faq.answer: The scanner is the first step and the cheapest part of the work. A hundred-page dump where half the findings do not apply is of no use. The value is in what comes after: verifying findings by hand, filtering false positives and setting priorities from your business's point of view.

faq.question: Is it safe for systems that are in use?
faq.answer: Yes. Any check that could affect operations is agreed separately and run in an agreed window or on a test copy. Everything else runs in observation mode and does not touch day-to-day work.

faq.question: What do we do with the report afterwards?
faq.answer: You can fix things yourselves — the report is written so your own administrator can work from it, not only its author. Or you can hand the remediation to us: that is separate work, and we always quote it before you decide.

faq.question: Will the protection get in the way of staff?
faq.answer: Badly configured protection will, and then people start working around it, which is worse than having none. That is why policies are introduced gradually and with a pilot: observation mode first, then a review of what fires needlessly, and only then blocking.

faq.question: Can we manage with locally available products?
faq.answer: Yes, and often it is a requirement rather than a choice. We select from what is available and supported in your market, and say plainly where a local equivalent is weaker and how to compensate.

faq.question: Do we have to start with an audit?
faq.answer: Not necessarily, but it helps: without understanding the risks, choosing tools turns into shopping from a list in an article. If the budget is limited, an audit helps spend it on what closes real holes.

faq.question: Who manages all this after the rollout?
faq.answer: By default, your team: we hand over configured systems, documentation and training. If you have no spare hands, managing it and triaging the alerts can be handed to us as a separate monitoring service.

infosecConsulting.lead: We put data handling in order both on paper and in practice: personal data and the law that governs it, notifying the regulator, policies and procedures, a threat model, preparation for an inspection. Without formal documents that do not match reality.

faq.question: Do we really have to notify the regulator?
faq.answer: Almost certainly yes: the obligation arises as soon as you process client and employee data, and very few exemptions remain. The difficulty is not the notification itself but making sure the purposes and categories of data it states match what you actually do.

faq.question: Is it enough to download a policy template from the internet?
faq.answer: As a document on the site, formally yes. As protection during an inspection, no: a template describes someone else's processes, and the first discrepancy with reality turns it from an argument into evidence. The documents have to describe what happens at your company.

faq.question: Do you only do documents, or the technical side too?
faq.answer: Both, but they are different pieces of work. Consulting answers "what should exist"; rolling out security tooling answers "how to make it so". We can close both parts or only the first, if your team handles the technical side.

faq.question: How long does it take?
faq.answer: A survey and a set of documents for a small company usually take a few weeks. Full compliance including technical measures stretches over months, so the work runs by priority: first what closes the most visible risk.

faq.question: How is this different from uptime monitoring?
faq.answer: Uptime monitoring answers "is the service running"; security monitoring answers "is anything suspicious happening to it". A service can run perfectly while handing data to someone who should not have it.

faq.question: Will you respond for us, or only report?
faq.answer: As agreed. The minimum is a notification with analysis and recommendations. The extended option is active steps under an agreed procedure: isolating a machine, locking an account, cutting access. The limits of authority are fixed in advance.

faq.question: Do we have to buy an expensive event collection system?
faq.answer: Not always. For a small infrastructure, open-source tooling is enough and a sensible place to start. An industrial system is justified when there are many sources and the volume of events stops fitting into simple tools.

faq.question: What if an incident has already happened?
faq.answer: Then the work starts with an investigation: how they got in, what they reached, what has to be closed immediately. Monitoring is set up afterwards — with rules for the scenario that actually happened to you.

faq.answer: Here we roll out a ready platform — faster and cheaper, and right for most companies. Building your own is for when nothing off the shelf meets the requirements: a special network, unusual integrations, or a messenger inside your own product. That is a separate service.

faq.question: How do you get staff to actually switch?
faq.answer: By not leaving parallel routes open. As long as an approval can be obtained in a private chat, nobody will go to the portal. So we move processes one at a time and together with the managers, rather than sending round an instruction and hoping.

faq.question: Can everything be deployed on our own servers?
faq.answer: Yes, many platforms have an on-premise option. It costs more to maintain, but the conversations and files stay with you — for some companies that is a hard requirement.

faq.question: How long does the rollout take?
faq.answer: A basic deployment with mail and structure takes weeks. Moving processes and habits across takes months, and that is normal: a platform switched on over a weekend usually stays empty.

faq.answer: A rollout takes a ready product and configures it for you — faster and cheaper, and the standard accounting is already there. faq.question: How many staff will need retraining?
faq.answer: Everyone who enters data, but differently: a salesperson needs one screen, an accountant the whole module. Training therefore runs by role rather than as one general lecture.

faq.question: Can it be rolled out in parts?
faq.answer: Yes, and usually that is wiser: one area first — sales or stock, say — then the next. Trying to launch everything at once most often ends with nothing working.

faq.answer: Often yes — through a controller, meters or external sensors, even if the machine has no modern interface. The survey gives the answer: sometimes recording the fact of running and stopping is enough, and that already answers the main question about downtime.

faq.question: Will this interfere with the line?

faq.question: Do we have to connect everything at once?

faq.question: Who owns the data collected?
